narrative:
The model estimated a 73% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and because that risk was high, your law school application was rejected. This is not a judgment that you cannot succeed; it means the academic profile in your application looked closer to students who did not pass on the first try.

The strongest factor was your class standing in the third year: you were in the third decile, compared with an average of about the sixth decile among accepted students. That relatively low rank pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second factor was your LSAT score of 31, below the accepted-student average of about 37; this also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than third-year standing. Third was your undergraduate GPA of 2.70, below the accepted average of about 3.23, adding further risk. Gender and race were not used in the prediction. Family income and full-time status were not among the top drivers.

To improve your chances, focus on the areas most associated with your predicted risk. Speak with an admissions adviser about whether retaking the LSAT after structured preparation or strengthening your academic record through additional coursework could help. Consider delaying reapplication, applying to programs with more holistic review, and asking whether an appeal or explanation of your record is possible. A concrete plan to raise your LSAT and demonstrate improved academic performance would be the most direct next step.
